source: Destatis Mikrozensus/Zensus 2022 (Eigentumsquote by Bundesland) + BBSR/IW Regionaler Preisindex 2022 (Kreis/city-level, not officially aggregated to Bundesland)
unit: mixed (thousands of households; index points, baseline=100)
notes: TIER B (Germany, per v2-plan.md classification: modeling/interpolation permitted if documented). This file combines TWO real primary-source Destatis/BBSR datasets that are NOT natively published at the same geographic granularity, requiring documented judgment calls: (1) HOMEOWNERSHIP RATE BY BUNDESLAND (16 states + national): REAL, unmodified figures from Destatis's official Mikrozensus/Zensus 2022 Eigentumsquote table (https://www.destatis.de/DE/Themen/Gesellschaft-Umwelt/Wohnen/Tabellen/tabelle-eigentumsquote.html), definition = share of owner-occupied dwellings among all occupied dwellings in residential buildings (excluding dormitories), household-level. This is a full, exact 16-state breakdown with no modeling required. Ranges from 15.9% (Berlin, a renter-dominated city-state) to 59.7% (Saarland). (2) REGIONAL PRICE INDEX (cost-of-living analog to BEA RPP): REAL BBSR/IW 'Regionaler Preisindex 2022' figures, but these are published ONLY at the COUNTY (Kreis) / independent-city level (401 units), covering over 85% of the CPI basket weight with a strong emphasis on modeled local rents (https://www.bbsr.bund.de/BBSR/DE/veroeffentlichungen/sonderveroeffentlichungen/2023/regionaler-preisindex-big-data.html), NOT officially aggregated to the 16-Bundesland level as of this pull -- the source PDF explicitly states 'Eine Tabelle mit dem Regionalen Preisindex als aggregiertem Wert je Bundesland ist nicht enthalten' (no Land-level aggregate table exists in the publication). Rather than fabricate a population-weighted Land-level average ourselves (which BBSR itself does not officially publish and which would require the full 401-county microdata file, not obtained within this task's step budget), we report: (a) individual COUNTY/CITY-LEVEL index values for ~15 major cities/counties spanning the extremes and each mapped to its Bundesland (see bbsr_city_examples in this notes field description; also directly embedded as a separate top-level object structure is NOT part of the 'rows' array to preserve schema conformance -- see raw reference data in build_de_laender_costs.py in the v2 directory for the full extracted table), and (b) BBSR's own East/West and urban/rural-settlement-type population-weighted aggregates, which are official and NOT modeled by us: national baseline=100.0; West Germany=100.8; East Germany=96.6; Top-7 cities (Berlin, Duesseldorf, Frankfurt am Main, Hamburg, Koeln, Muenchen, Stuttgart)=111.5; large cities excl. Top-7=100.6; urban counties=99.9; rural counties with some density=96.4; sparsely populated rural counties=95.1. The 'regional_price_index_2022_baseline_100' field in the per-Bundesland 'rows' array is left NULL for all 16 states rather than populated with a fabricated/interpolated Land-average, per the task's 'do not fabricate' instruction; the v2 frontend should instead use a look-up against the city/county examples plus the BBSR settlement-type aggregates as a reasonable proxy, or obtain the full BBSR county microdata file directly (available for purchase/request from BBSR, not freely downloadable as CSV) for an exact population-weighted Land aggregation if higher precision is required. GENERAL PATTERN (documented in the source, useful even without a Land aggregate): prices are systematically higher in southern/western urban areas (Bayern, Baden-Wuerttemberg, Hessen -- home to 8 of the top 10 most expensive counties) and lower in eastern rural areas (16 of the 22 lowest-price counties are in Ostdeutschland: Sachsen, Sachsen-Anhalt, Thueringen, Brandenburg); Munich has by far the highest cost of living in Germany at 125.1 (25.1% above the national average), while the cheapest rural areas (Vogtlandkreis in Sachsen; Greiz in Thueringen) sit at 90.5 (9.5% below average) -- a much narrower urban/rural spread than the roughly 30-40 percentage-point range seen across US BEA state RPPs, consistent with Germany's more compressed regional cost structure. This file is intended to pair with de_evs.json (national-level EVS/LWR consumption-by-income data) to let the v2 frontend apply a state-like Land/city cost-of-living multiplier and an income-appropriate homeownership assumption, analogous to how us_rpp_state.json and us_rpp_metro.json are used alongside us_ces_2024_by_decile.json for the United States.
